Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the classic clinical presentation of patients with various types of bone tumors.
Identify the differential diagnosis for bone-forming tumors based on patient age, body region,
and bone location.
Clinical Presentation
Overview
The clinical presentation of bone tumors is highly variable, with some patients presenting with
an incidentally identified lesion and other patients presenting with a history of pain or a
palpable mass.

Patient History
A thorough family history aids in identifying risk factors for bone lesions and multifocal
involvement. A family history of multiple hereditary exostosis aids in assessing palpable
masses or gradual deformity in young children, whereas a patient history of
retinoblastoma increases the risk of osteosarcoma.
Physical Examination
Pathologic fracture
Palpable mass
Tenderness to palpation
Gradual or acute deformity
Skin lesions (café au lait spots)

Physical Examination
Benign lesions cannot be distinguished from malignant lesions based on the patient
history and physical examination alone. Benign non-ossifying fibromas and highly
malignant osteosarcomas may have nearly identical presentations despite tremendous
variability in presentation.

Evaluation of all patients begins with a detailed history and physical examination.
Although pain is a concerning symptom, it is not diagnostic of a malignant or benign
process nor of a large or small lesion. Pain may be caused by a small lesion, especially if
in proximity to a joint, musculature is being tethered, nerves are compressed, or the
lesion is cortically based and expanding the periosteum. Referred pain or radicular pain
deceptively draws attention away from the site of concern, such as in pelvic and spine
lesions, in which nerves may be compressed proximally and the symptoms may be
radicular. Pain because of mechanical stress on the bone typically is worse with weight
bearing and increased activity, whereas pathophysiologic pain typically occurs at odd
and/or random times. Pathologic pain is caused by tumor cellular activity (such as in
fibrous dysplasia or malignancy) and the surrounding edema/inflammation (such as in
osteoblastoma and osteochondromas) and often presents unrelated to activity or at
night or awakens the patient from sleep. The chronicity, frequency, and relief of pain are
critical to determine. Classically, approximately 80% of patients with osteoid osteoma
experience consistent pain relief with NSAIDs, which is nearly pathognomic, whereas a
vague history of waxing and waning pain for many years is consistent with fibrous
dysplasia.
Constitutional symptoms, such as fever, chills, fatigue, weight loss, rash, and headache,
are present with benign and malignant conditions, such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis
and Ewing sarcoma, respectively, and do not confer a malignant versus benign diagnosis,
especially in children, because these constitutional symptoms also may be present with
infection, leukemia, and lymphoma. Constitutional symptoms may guide but not confirm
diagnosis.
Presentation with a pathologic fracture is not definitive for a malignant or benign
condition. Typically, a pathologic fracture occurs through the lesion because of
mechanical weakening of the osseous structure. A pathologic fracture at the site of a
lesion may obfuscate patient workup because it makes radiographic and pathologic
assessment difficult to interpret given the presence of fracture fragments, edema,
hematoma, and callus at variable stages of fracture healing. Care must be taken to
ensure that a biopsy is appropriately performed of pathologic tissue rather than fracture
callus.

Gradual deformity may be caused by various underlying conditions, most of which are
benign, such as multiple hereditary exostosis, Ollier disease, osteofibrous dysplasia,
fibrous dysplasia, aneurysmal bone cyst, and unicameral bone cyst.
Initial Workup
Imaging Studies
Radiographs of entire bone
MRI with and without contrast of entire bone
Chest CT scan
Positron emission tomography scan or bone scan of the entire body
Laboratory Studies
Complete blood count with differential
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
C-reactive protein level
Alkaline phosphatase level
Lactate dehydrogenase level
Comprehensive metabolic panel
